key.explanation: Value has to be communicated in the order the buyer moves through: make the problem and the relevant value understandable first, then introduce alternatives and proof as the decision approaches. Arriving with proof first is arriving too early.

One purchase can stack a functional need, an emotional one and a social one at once, and the commuter names all three without using the words. Naming the product, the frequency or the price answers a different question.

Functional requirements say what the system does; quality requirements — performance, security, availability — say how well and under what conditions. The 30-second bound and the role restriction constrain the export the first statement introduces.

Collection should be limited to a stated purpose, protection built in by default rather than on request, and a third-party processor's compliance verified before data reaches it. Collecting now for a feature that may never exist fails the first of those.

Definition is what the product does and is largely internal, for the team and its partners to build against. Positioning is how it changes things for the user and why they should care. One sentence cannot be both.

The mainstream buyer needs a complete offer: the product plus references, reliability and support. Concentrating on one narrow segment is what makes that complete offer achievable and the references credible.

The method sorts necessity, and it only works if the categories are used: naming what will not be done is what makes the ordering real. A regulatory mandate is a constraint on the release rather than a candidate within it.

Cost-based pricing is the fallback for when the deployment and the customer's economics are unknown. Here both are known and quantified, so the price should be set against the ₹2.4 crore of value created.
Traceability and an adaptable roadmap let new evidence change delivery without losing strategic direction.
Premium, skimming, penetration, bundling and freemium are distinct pricing strategies, each fitting a different market position and a different objective.
An MVP buys maximum learning for minimum effort, and what it measures decides the pivot: product, segment or value.
A product line is the set of variants built over one common platform architecture, with a similar look and feel but different functionality per market or device.

A roadmap is a statement of intent rather than a release plan, and its planning horizons and format follow the context — fixed dates where customers must plan deployments, rolling themes where they need not.
A physical product is made of atoms and a software product of bits, and the differences follow from that: marginal cost, iteration speed, distribution and how fast feedback arrives.
Product lifecycle management runs conception, market introduction, growth, maturity, decline and withdrawal, and what product management should be spending on changes at every stage.
Marginal cost is what one more unit or user costs to serve: high for atoms, which consume material, manufacturing and logistics, and close to zero for bits.
Value communication must always match the buyer's stage: the need, evidence, format and channel useful at that moment.
Product marketing management owns positioning, segmentation, messaging, go-to-market, launches and advocacy — the articulation of value — while product management owns the life cycle.

Responsible product management maximises value while minimising harm, and its named hazards are dark patterns that trick users, AI bias inherited from historical data, and models without explainability or a human in the loop.
A product platform is a foundational set of shared technologies, components and services enabling multiple related products to be developed, not a product itself.

Release planning decides which requirements go into which version and when it ships, weighing customer pull, engineering readiness, dependencies on hardware or platform, and the competing pressures on the date.

Contracts, service level agreements, intellectual property and open-source licences are product decisions: licence scope, uptime, data residency and indemnification all constrain what the product may do.

Across the funding stages what an investor asks for changes: problem clarity at idea stage, activation and retention at MVP, scalability at product-market fit, share and roadmap at growth, and predictability at maturity.
A revenue model answers who pays, for what, how often and why they keep paying, and software's two poles are the one-time charge licence and recurring subscription.

Software product management governs a product across its whole life cycle to deliver customer and business value, and the evolution of software product management runs from the production era through marketing, software, platforms and today's intelligent products.
Premium, skimming, penetration, bundling and freemium are distinct pricing strategies, each fitting a different market position and a different objective.
Customer discovery runs three steps — spot the customer's problem, survey a large enough sample to find the pattern and its segment, then study the alternatives people already use.
MoSCoW sorts necessity and RICE compares reach, impact, confidence and effort; neither ever replaces judgement.
The B2C value pyramid stacks functional value at the base, then emotional value, then life-changing and social-impact elements at the top.
Lean Canvas adapts one-page modelling to early uncertainty, treating every box as an assumption still to be tested.
A sourcing strategy decides what a team builds and what it buys or outsources, across talent, make-versus-buy, infrastructure and data — and keeps in-house whatever carries the competitive advantage.

Software product management governs a product across its whole life cycle to deliver customer and business value, and the evolution of software product management runs from the production era through marketing, software, platforms and today's intelligent products.
Crossing to mainstream customers always requires a focused beachhead, a complete experience, references and lower adoption risk.
A product opportunity must be wanted by customers, technically achievable, and economically sustainable; strength in only two dimensions leaves a predictable failure.
A product talks through its features and the company talks through its price, so a price signals the value definition, the risk posture and who the offer is for.

₹1,800 a year against ₹5,400 is a three-year payback, and four years of retention gives about ₹7,200 of lifetime gross profit. Both facts are true at once, and the second does not remove the cash risk the first creates.

Total is everyone the product could in principle serve, 900,000. Certification is a real constraint that narrows it to 90,000 serviceable. The obtainable figure is bounded by both competition and the firm's own reach, which is why 4,000 is the number a plan should be built on.

Competition is whatever the customer would otherwise do about this job - here a spreadsheet, a person, and doing nothing at all, which between them cover thirty-five of the forty teams. Adjacent software serving a different need is not an alternative.

Registrations, page views and press mentions accumulate and cannot fall, so they cannot tell progress from activity. Flat weekly active use is the figure that would answer whether the product works, and a number with no owner and no threshold cannot trigger anything.
A roadmap translates strategy into a sequence of releases on a time axis. Deferral is part of that decision, which is why an inventory of eventual contents is a different artefact.

Customer requirements are business needs and aspirations; the product requirement is what the product will do about them; project requirements break that down for a release. Standardising is what turns one hospital's need into something many can buy.

Desirability and feasibility both hold; viability fails, because ₹400 of revenue against ₹430 of cost means every additional driver loses money and the case states the cost does not fall with scale. All three checks have to clear.
The canvas exists to make assumptions explicit and cheap to change. Holding it stable to look consistent is the one use that removes its value.

ARPU spreads revenue across the user base and customer lifetime value covers the whole relationship. Gross margin sits before below-the-line costs, and NPS is one of the steadier-state measures a startup cannot yet lean on.
The unit follows the customer relationship model. SaaS acquires a customer who transacts repeatedly, so the account is the unit; a marketplace relationship is transactional, so the transaction is.
TAM measures the prize, SAM what you are permitted and able to reach, SOM what you can take given who already holds it. They are narrowing constraints, not a headline figure.

Metrics exist to reduce uncertainty and improve decisions with the information available. Standard performance measures assume a steadier state than an early-stage product has, which is why the startup case differs.
Customers set the comparison, and in enterprise the most common alternative is inertia — doing nothing at all. Defining competition early and narrowly is named as the biggest mistake.
The four are beachhead focus, simplification, trust and reliability, and ecosystem fit. Mainstream customers avoid risk, so the work is lowering perceived risk rather than signalling through price.

Cost-based pricing prices your inputs — hourly billing worked back from salary — and is defensible only in ignorance of deployment and impact. A measurable peg is what lets you price the outcome instead.
Problem, solution, key metrics, and unfair advantage are the Lean Canvas additions. Customer segments, channels, cost structure, and revenue structure carry across from the Business Model Canvas.
The evolution is deliberate ordering, not accident: the team launched on iPhone knowing many users were on Android. A roadmap is a smart sequence for developing, releasing, and evolving a solution.
The split is action versus quality. Sending is the action and so functional; the 200-millisecond bound is a quality and so non-functional, constraining architecture rather than behaviour.

Each area needs a different skill — design for desirability, engineering for feasibility, business for viability. A prototype proves you can build it, which is the feasibility question; viability asks whether it can profit or fund the business.
MoSCoW is an acronym — must, should, could, won't — used as a filter rather than a ranking. Naming what won't be done is the half that makes scope control real.
